title: Working Capital: The Investment Most SMEs Don't Realise They're Making

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Six months ago, Ramesh nearly ran out of cash in his best month ever.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Today, the news is even better.

lines.speaker: V
lines.name: Vikram
lines.text: Sir, Sharma Retail has signed! Twenty lakh of orders, every single month!

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The office is celebrating again.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And this time, Lata has done her homework before anyone asked.

lines.speaker: L
lines.name: Lata
lines.text: Sir, this order will earn us about five lakh a month. But before the first rupee comes in, we will need nearly forty lakh more.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Forty lakh. Not for a new godown. Not for a new van. Just to keep the business running.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Welcome to working capital: the investment most businesses don't realise they're making.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: When most people think about investment, they think about things they can see. A new machine. A delivery vehicle. An office renovation.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: When Ramesh bought his van last year, everyone could see where the money went.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Working capital is different. You don't see it. You don't cut a ribbon for it. You don't announce it on social media.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Yet every business invests in it, every single day.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Think about everything Ramesh pays for before Sharma Retail pays him.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The stock is bought. The staff are paid. The godown rent is due. The trucks are loaded, and the diesel is paid for. The invoice goes out.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And only then does the customer eventually make payment.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Between spending money and receiving money, there is a gap.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Working capital funds that gap.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Follow one rupee through Ramesh's business.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On day one, it buys stock from Kapoor, who gives thirty days' credit.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On day thirty, Ramesh pays Kapoor, and the stock goes out to Sharma Retail.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Sharma Retail pays in sixty days.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So the rupee leaves Ramesh's bank on day thirty, and comes back on day ninety. For sixty days, it is working somewhere else.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Then the cycle repeats.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The question is not whether the cycle exists. The question is how efficiently it is being managed.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Now multiply that rupee by twenty lakh a month.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Sixty days of sales waiting with Sharma Retail: forty lakh.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: One month of extra stock in the godown: fifteen lakh.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Kapoor's credit covers fifteen lakh of that.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: What is left, forty lakh, has to come from Ramesh, or from his bank.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Many owners naturally assume that higher sales will automatically improve financial strength. In reality, growth often demands additional working capital.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: More stock, more staff, more trucks on the road, more credit to customers, all paid for long before the money comes back.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So, in the month of his biggest order, Ramesh sits down with his bank manager to ask for a higher limit.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Not because the business was failing. Because the business was growing.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Here is what most owners miss. Working capital is not a number the accountant finds at month-end.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It is created by decisions made all over the business: in sales, in purchase, in dispatch and in collections.

lines.speaker: V
lines.name: Vikram
lines.text: Sir, Sharma Retail is asking for ninety days instead of sixty.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Thirty more days of credit on twenty lakh a month: another twenty lakh waiting.

lines.speaker: K
lines.name: Kapoor
lines.text: Ramesh bhai, take three months' stock now, and I'll give you two percent off.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Two percent off sounds good. It also puts thirty lakh more on Ramesh's shelves.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A truck held up for a week means an invoice raised a week late, and cash a week late.

lines.speaker: M
lines.name: Mr. Mehta
lines.text: Rameshji, you know my payment is always safe. Next month, definitely.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Thirty days late on fifteen lakh: fifteen lakh more, waiting.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: What appears in the financial statements is often the result of decisions being made throughout the business.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Lata does not run a complicated formula. Every Monday, she asks four questions.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: How quickly are customers paying?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: How much stock are we carrying?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Are we buying more than we need?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: How long does a rupee take to come back?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Those questions usually reveal more than a spreadsheet ever will.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: So Ramesh holds Sharma Retail at sixty days.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: He thanks Kapoor, and buys one month's stock, not three.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And he arranges the bank limit before the first truck leaves, not on a Friday afternoon in a panic.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Three months later, Sharma Retail's payments start arriving, on time. Salaries went out on the first of every month.

lines.speaker: L
lines.name: Lata
lines.text: Sir, same order, same profit. The only difference is that this time, we knew the money would be away for sixty days.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At SanMitra, we built OfficeMitra for exactly these Monday questions. It reads your existing Tally or Zoho books, read-only, on your own computer, and shows how quickly customers are paying, who is overdue and what you owe suppliers, on one screen.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Working capital is not idle money. It is not excess cash sitting in a bank account. It is the fuel that allows operations to continue between the moment money is spent and the moment money is received.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Because in the end, working capital is simply the cost of keeping the wheels turning.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Try this this week. Take your five biggest customers, and check how many days each actually took to pay, compared with the terms you agreed.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Then ask your stores team which items have not moved in ninety days.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: This is OfficeMitra Finance Insights. Tell me in the comments: in your business, where does money wait the longest? Next time: why growing businesses run out of cash.
